primary_references: Holland et al. 2004; Yovel et al. 2011; Boonman et al. 2014
notes: Old World fruit bats orient by sight and smell rather than sonar, with large forward-facing eyes and no laryngeal echolocation. Rousettus is the one genus known to echolocate and has its own entry.
curation_note: Species-level records should use evidence_class=not_applicable unless the genus is a known click-echolocator. Wing-generated clicks reported in a few genera by Boonman et al. 2014 are a different mechanism and are not asserted as echolocation here.

call_structure: CF-FM: long constant-frequency component with terminal (and usually initial) FM sweep; second harmonic dominant
primary_references: Schnitzler & Kalko 2001; Jones & Teeling 2006; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013
notes: CF frequency is the diagnostic parameter and is unusually stable within populations; strong geographic and sexual variation in some species. Range low end from large SE Asian species; high end from small species such as R. hipposideros and relatives.

call_structure: CF-FM: shorter CF component than Rhinolophidae with terminal FM; second harmonic dominant
primary_references: Schnitzler & Kalko 2001; Jones & Teeling 2006; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013
notes: Doppler shift compensation reported as partial or absent in some taxa. Low end from large Macronycteris/Hipposideros; high end from small Hipposideros.

call_structure: CF-FM
primary_references: Foley et al. 2015 (family delimitation); Fenton & Bell literature on Cloeotis
notes: Contains the highest CF frequency known in bats (Cloeotis percivali, ~212 kHz). Most species in the family have no published call description. The lower bound is set by the larger Malagasy Triaenops, whose males call near 82 kHz.
curation_note: Split from Hipposideridae; check that your MDD version recognises this family. Lower bound reduced from 90 to 80 kHz: published Triaenops menamena males call at about 82 kHz, below the previous bound.

call_structure: short multiharmonic broadband FM emitted at low intensity
primary_references: Schnitzler & Kalko 2001; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013
notes: Passive-listening gleaners; echolocation is often secondary to prey-generated sound, so peak frequency is a weak descriptor of foraging behaviour.

call_structure: short steep FM with narrowband component
primary_references: Surlykke et al. 1993
notes: Monotypic family (Craseonycteris thonglongyai); the family row and the species row are the same datum.

call_structure: short multiharmonic FM/QCF
primary_references: Habersetzer 1981; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013

call_structure: low-intensity multiharmonic steep FM
primary_references: Schnitzler & Kalko 2001
notes: Gleaners; low source levels mean the family is under-sampled by passive acoustic monitoring and the published range is likely incomplete.

call_structure: narrowband QCF or shallow FM with multiple harmonics; often multi-harmonic search calls
primary_references: Kalko 1995; Jung et al. 2007; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013
notes: Neotropical taxa relatively well described; African and Asian taxa much less so. The upper bound is set by small high-frequency taxa: Rhynchonycteris naso calls at about 100 kHz in search phase, well above the 60 kHz this row previously gave.
curation_note: Upper bound raised from 60 to 105 kHz after a measured R. naso value of 89.7 kHz was flagged against it and the published search-phase figure of ~100 kHz confirmed the range, not the datum, was wrong.

call_structure: mixed CF/QCF component followed by FM sweep (trawling)
primary_references: Kalko et al. 1998; Schnitzler & Kalko 2001
notes: Only two species; both reasonably well described.

call_structure: mostly LDC FM/QCF; the Pteronotus parnellii complex is HDC CF-FM
primary_references: Kossl et al. 1999; Schnitzler & Kalko 2001; Clare et al. 2013
notes: The Pteronotus parnellii complex is the only oral-emitting high-duty-cycle lineage known; all other mormoopids are low duty cycle.
curation_note: Do NOT propagate the family duty_cycle_class to species. Set duty_cycle at species level or leave unknown.

call_structure: short low-intensity broadband multiharmonic FM
primary_references: Kalko 1995; Brinklov et al. 2009; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013
notes: Very low source levels; many species are effectively undetectable by standard passive monitoring, so published parameters come mostly from hand-released or flight-tent recordings. Frugivores and nectarivores are poorly represented.

call_structure: broadband FM, high frequency
primary_references: scattered Neotropical call libraries; no family-level review
curation_note: Treat any species-level value as provisional and flag prominently as a knowledge gap.

call_structure: short broadband FM
primary_references: scattered Neotropical call libraries; no family-level review

call_structure: FM; poorly characterised
primary_references: Ralisata et al. and scattered Malagasy surveys
notes: Two species, both Madagascar-endemic; almost no published acoustic data. A clear gap to display.

call_structure: low-frequency broadband FM/QCF with unusual harmonic structure
primary_references: Parsons 1997
notes: Ground-foraging; calls differ structurally from typical aerial hawkers.

call_structure: long narrowband QCF search calls, often alternating between frequency bands
primary_references: Schnitzler & Kalko 2001; Jung et al. 2014
notes: Open-space aerial hawkers; long-range low-frequency calls. Alternating call types within a sequence make single peak-frequency values misleading.

call_structure: FM-QCF
primary_references: Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013; regional African and Asian call libraries
notes: Taxonomically split into many cryptic species whose calls overlap heavily; species-level assignment from acoustics alone is often not defensible.

call_structure: broadband FM
primary_references: Lack et al. 2010 (family delimitation); southern African call libraries
notes: Two species, southern Africa; minimal published acoustic data.

call_structure: steep broadband FM, high frequency
primary_references: scattered Neotropical and Caribbean call libraries

call_structure: highly variable: steep broadband FM (clutter foragers) through FM-QCF to narrowband QCF (open space)
primary_references: Schnitzler & Kalko 2001; Jones & Teeling 2006; Denzinger & Schnitzler 2013
notes: The family-level range is so wide that it carries almost no information for an individual species. Low end: Euderma maculatum ~10 kHz. High end: Kerivoula spp., whose start frequencies exceed 200 kHz.
curation_note: Prefer genus-level inference where you can justify it, and say plainly on the page that the family default is uninformative here.
